newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Global Telecom pact sealed, seen boosting world economy.
newsitem.headline: Global Telecom pact sealed, seen boosting world economy.

text.p: Key countries around the globe agreed on Saturday on a landmark pact opening up most of the world's $600 billion telecommunications market and hailed as offering a major boost to the international economy.

The deal came after hours of last-minute haggling when the United States made known it would come on board, bringing an end to over three years of on-off negotiations to bring free trade principles to the booming telecoms sector.

"We are celebrating a very important victory," a beaming Renato Ruggiero, Director-General of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), told a news conference just after officials from 68 countries had signalled their assent.

The deal, he declared, "will bring lower costs for consumers around the world, both ordinary people and businesses, and will be especially beneficial for the development of the world's poorest countries".
In Washington, President Bill Clinton said the accord, covering nearly 93 per cent of the global telecoms market, "will bring clear benefits to American workers, businesses and consumers alike".

Both Clinton and Ruggiero said that, combined with completion expected next month of a world pact on freeing trade in information technology products, if would spread the technological revolution to the farthest corner of the globe.
Under the accord, signatory states will open up long-protected government or private national monopolies to competition from both foreign and domestic firms based on commitments subject to WTO rules.
For the first time it will bring services such as satellite systems, cellular phones, data transmission and paging under the umbrella of the trade watchdog and its dispute settlement system.

Neil McMillan, chairman of the WTO negotiating group which finally clinched the deal, said this would bring the predictability and stability to the market that was sought by investors as well as by the big global telecoms companies.
Ruggiero said liberalising telecoms could boost income for the industry by some $1 trillion over the next decade -- or around four per cent of total current global economic output.

The success in the talks would also ease conclusion of another long-sought WTO deal later this year to open up financial services -- including banking and insurance -- to global competition, he added.

U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky said in Washington that the pact would create up to a million new U.S. jobs not only in telecom companies but also in industries such as software and electronic publishing.

European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, speaking just before it was finalised, said the pact -- to go into force once ratified by national legislatures -- would give a massive bounce also to firms around the globe producing high-technology telecoms equipment.
U.S. industry and congressional groups immediately welcomed the deal, which is also seen as a big boost to the credibility of the fledgling, two-year-old WTO.

"We commend the WTO for its work in getting us an international trade agreement that opens markets and increases foreign investment," the Global Information Infrastructure Commission, a broad U.S. telecoms industry coalition, said in a statement.
"This agreement lays the foundation for significant new investment in informatics and telecommunications infrastructure in nations around the world," it added.
